claim: In C. elegans, the CELF family RBP UNC-75 is required for axon regeneration.
source: In C. elegans the CELF (CUGBP and Etr-3 Like Factor) family RBP UNC-75 is required for axon regeneration.
evidence: The abstract directly states this finding, which is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1.

claim: UNC-75 regulates alternative splicing of two mRNA isoforms of the SNARE Syntaxin/unc-64.
source: In particular, we show that UNC-75 regulates alternative splicing of two mRNA isoforms of the SNARE Syntaxin/unc-64.
evidence: This is demonstrated through CLIP-seq data (Figure 3A), RT-qPCR (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A), and splicing reporter assays (Figure 3E).

claim: In C. elegans mutants lacking unc-75, regenerating axons form growth cones yet are deficient in extension.
source: In C. elegans mutants lacking unc-75 or its targets, regenerating axons form growth cones, yet are deficient in extension.
evidence: This is shown through microscopy images (Figure 1A, D) and quantification (Figure 1B, C, Figure 1—figure supplement 2).

claim: Mouse Celf2 expression is upregulated after peripheral nerve injury.
source: Further, mRNAs for several Syntaxins show CELF2 dependent regulation. Our data delineate a post-transcriptional regulatory pathway with a conserved role in regenerative axon extension.
evidence: RT-qPCR data shows Celf2 transcript levels significantly increase in DRGs after sciatic nerve crush (Figure 6C).

claim: Celf2 mutant mice are defective in axon regeneration.
source: Extending these findings to mammalian axon regeneration, we show that mouse Celf2 expression is upregulated after peripheral nerve injury and that Celf2 mutant mice are defective in axon regeneration.
evidence: This is demonstrated through in vivo sciatic nerve regeneration assays showing reduced SCG10 positive axons in Celf2 mutants (Figure 6D, E).

claim: PLM axon regeneration in unc-75 mutants was reduced to 30–40% of wild type levels.
source: PLM axon regeneration in unc-75 mutants was reduced to 30–40% of wild type levels (Figure 1A,B).
evidence: Quantitative data from laser axotomy experiments is shown in Figure 1B.

claim: unc-75(md1344), a small deletion affecting the last exon encoding part of RRM3 and a nuclear localization signal, displayed impairment in regrowth equivalent to the null mutants.
source: Interestingly, unc-75(md1344), a small deletion affecting the last exon encoding part of RRM3 and a nuclear localization signal (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A), displayed impairment in regrowth equivalent to the null mutants (Figure 1A,B).
evidence: This is shown through quantification of PLM axon regrowth (Figure 1B) and molecular characterization of the deletion (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).

claim: Nuclear localization may be critical for UNC-75 function in axon regeneration.
source: Transgenic animals expressing Pmec-4-GFP::UNC-75ΔNLS(aa 1–472) showed diffuse fluorescence throughout the cell, as compared to full-length GFP::UNC-75, which localizes to neuronal nuclei (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B) (Loria et al., 2003), suggesting that nuclear localization may be critical for UNC-75 function in axon regeneration.
evidence: This inference is based on localization data (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B) and the observation that the NLS deletion mutant fails to rescue (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).

claim: In wild type, around 35% of DD2 commissures and 50% of VD4 commissures regrow to the dorsal cord by 24 hr after axotomy.
source: In wild type, around 35% of DD2 commissures and 50% of VD4 commissures regrow to the dorsal cord by 24 hr after axotomy, whereas in unc-75 mutants fewer than 10% of commissures regrew to the dorsal cord (Figure 1E).
evidence: Quantitative data from motor neuron regeneration experiments is shown in Figure 1E.

claim: In unc-75 mutants fewer than 10% of commissures regrew to the dorsal cord.
source: In wild type, around 35% of DD2 commissures and 50% of VD4 commissures regrow to the dorsal cord by 24 hr after axotomy, whereas in unc-75 mutants fewer than 10% of commissures regrew to the dorsal cord (Figure 1E).
evidence: Quantitative data from motor neuron regeneration experiments is shown in Figure 1E.

claim: UNC-75 is critical for regenerative regrowth of multiple neuron types.
source: Thus UNC-75 is critical for regenerative regrowth of multiple neuron types.
evidence: This conclusion is based on data showing defects in both PLM sensory neurons (Figure 1A-D) and GABAergic motor neurons (Figure 1E).

claim: The unc-75(e950) PLM regrowth defect is rescued by multicopy and single copy unc-75(+) transgenes.
source: The unc-75(e950) PLM regrowth defect is rescued by multicopy and single copy unc-75(+) transgenes.
evidence: Rescue data is shown in Figure 1B with quantification of PLM axon regrowth.

claim: Expression of UNC-75 using a touch neuron specific promoter (Pmec-4) fully rescued PLM regrowth.
source: Moreover, expression of UNC-75 using a touch neuron specific promoter (Pmec-4) fully rescued PLM regrowth, indicating that UNC-75 acts cell-autonomously (Figure 1A,B).
evidence: Cell-autonomous rescue is demonstrated through transgenic rescue experiments shown in Figure 1A, B.

claim: UNC-75 acts cell-autonomously in axon regeneration.
source: Moreover, expression of UNC-75 using a touch neuron specific promoter (Pmec-4) fully rescued PLM regrowth, indicating that UNC-75 acts cell-autonomously (Figure 1A,B).
evidence: This is inferred from the ability of cell-specific expression to rescue the phenotype (Figure 1A, B).

claim: Expression of UNC-75 in wild type animals did not enhance regrowth.
source: Expression of UNC-75 in wild type animals did not enhance regrowth, indicating that UNC-75 is necessary but not sufficient to promote axon regeneration (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is shown through overexpression experiments quantified in Figure 1B.

claim: UNC-75 is necessary but not sufficient to promote axon regeneration.
source: Expression of UNC-75 in wild type animals did not enhance regrowth, indicating that UNC-75 is necessary but not sufficient to promote axon regeneration (Figure 1B).
evidence: This conclusion is inferred from the observation that overexpression does not enhance wild-type regeneration (Figure 1B).

claim: In unc-75 mutant neurons the rate of axon extension was reduced at multiple time points after injury.
source: In unc-75 mutant neurons the rate of axon extension was reduced at multiple time points after injury (Figure 1C), despite the presence of growth cones at the tip of the regrowing axons (Figure 1A).
evidence: Time course data showing reduced regrowth at 6, 16, 24, and 48 hours is presented in Figure 1C.

claim: Wild-type PLM regenerative growth cones tended to be small and transient, and converted rapidly to elongating axons.
source: Using time-lapse imaging we found that wild-type PLM regenerative growth cones tended to be small and transient, and converted rapidly to elongating axons.
evidence: This is observed through time-lapse imaging shown in Figure 1D and Videos 1-2.

claim: In unc-75 mutants, regenerative growth cones frequently displayed dynamic filopodial protrusions, but these did not drive long-range axon extension.
source: In contrast, unc-75 mutants frequently displayed regenerative growth cones with dynamic filopodial protrusions, but these did not drive long-range axon extension (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D and Video 1,2).
evidence: This is demonstrated through time-lapse imaging shown in Figure 1D and Videos 1-2.

claim: Growth cones were observed more frequently in non-regenerating PLM axons in unc-75 mutants than in the wild type.
source: Indeed, we observed growth cones more frequently in non-regenerating PLM axons in unc-75 mutants than in the wild type (Figure 1—figure supplement 2), consistent with previous observations that presence of a growth cone does not correlate highly with axon extension (Chen et al., 2011; Edwards and Hammarlund, 2014).
evidence: Quantification of growth cone frequency is shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2B.

claim: Presence of a growth cone does not correlate highly with axon extension.
source: Indeed, we observed growth cones more frequently in non-regenerating PLM axons in unc-75 mutants than in the wild type (Figure 1—figure supplement 2), consistent with previous observations that presence of a growth cone does not correlate highly with axon extension (Chen et al., 2011; Edwards and Hammarlund, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work and the current observation in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: UNC-75 is required for regenerative axon extension but is either dispensable or a negative regulator of regenerative growth cone formation.
source: Thus UNC-75 is required for regenerative axon extension but is either dispensable or a negative regulator of regenerative growth cone formation.
evidence: This conclusion is inferred from the observation that unc-75 mutants form growth cones but fail to extend axons (Figure 1A, D, E, Figure 1—figure supplement 2).

claim: The C. elegans Elav-like RNA binding protein EXC-7 functions partially redundantly with UNC-75 in synaptic transmission.
source: The C. elegans Elav-like RNA binding protein EXC-7 functions partially redundantly with UNC-75 in synaptic transmission (Loria et al., 2003), and co-regulates overlapping mRNA splicing events (Norris et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: exc-7 mutants displayed normal PLM axon regeneration.
source: exc-7 mutants displayed normal PLM axon regeneration, and unc-75 exc-7 double mutants resembled unc-75 single mutants in regeneration (Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: Quantitative data is shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3A.

claim: unc-75 exc-7 double mutants resembled unc-75 single mutants in regeneration.
source: exc-7 mutants displayed normal PLM axon regeneration, and unc-75 exc-7 double mutants resembled unc-75 single mutants in regeneration (Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: Quantitative data is shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3A.

claim: fox-1/RBFOX is not required for PLM regrowth.
source: fox-1/RBFOX, another known interactor of unc-75 in neuronal alternative splicing (Kuroyanagi et al., 2013a), is also not required for PLM regrowth (Chen et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: UNC-75 functions in axon regeneration non-redundantly with known neuronal splicing regulators EXC-7 and FOX-1.
source: These observations suggest UNC-75 functions in axon regeneration non-redundantly with these known neuronal splicing regulators.
evidence: This is inferred from genetic interaction data showing that exc-7 and fox-1 mutants have normal regeneration (Figure 1—figure supplement 3A and citation).

claim: PLM and motor neuron axon regeneration is completely blocked in null mutants of dlk-1.
source: In C. elegans, PLM and motor neuron axon regeneration is completely blocked in null mutants of dlk-1 and is increased in animals overexpressing active DLK-1 (Yan and Jin, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Axon regeneration is increased in animals overexpressing active DLK-1.
source: In C. elegans, PLM and motor neuron axon regeneration is completely blocked in null mutants of dlk-1 and is increased in animals overexpressing active DLK-1 (Yan and Jin, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Double mutants unc-75(0); dlk-1(0) did not further reduce PLM axon regrowth compared to dlk-1(0).
source: Double mutants unc-75(0); dlk-1(0) did not further reduce PLM axon regrowth compared to dlk-1(0), and the regrowing axons had no regenerative growth cones, resembling dlk-1(0) (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A,3B).
evidence: Quantitative data is shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3B.

claim: Overexpression of DLK-1 in unc-75(0) partially improved regrowth compared to unc-75(0) single mutants.
source: Overexpression of DLK-1 in unc-75(0) partially improved regrowth compared to unc-75(0) single mutants (Figure 1—figure supplement 3C), suggesting that unc-75 and dlk-1 likely function in parallel.
evidence: Quantitative data is shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3C.

claim: unc-75 and dlk-1 likely function in parallel pathways.
source: Overexpression of DLK-1 in unc-75(0) partially improved regrowth compared to unc-75(0) single mutants (Figure 1—figure supplement 3C), suggesting that unc-75 and dlk-1 likely function in parallel.
evidence: This is inferred from genetic interaction data (Figure 1—figure supplement 3B, C).

claim: Loss of EFA-6 strongly enhances PLM axon regrowth.
source: The conserved protein EFA-6 regulates axonal microtubule dynamics, and loss of EFA-6 strongly enhances PLM axon regrowth (Chen et al., 2011; 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: efa-6(0) partially rescued unc-75(0) PLM regrowth defects.
source: efa-6(0) partially rescued unc-75(0) PLM regrowth defects (Figure 1—figure supplement 3C), but not the growth cone phenotype (Figure 1—figure supplement 2), suggesting that EFA-6 and UNC-75 function in parallel.
evidence: Quantitative data is shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3C.

claim: EFA-6 and UNC-75 function in parallel pathways.
source: efa-6(0) partially rescued unc-75(0) PLM regrowth defects (Figure 1—figure supplement 3C), but not the growth cone phenotype (Figure 1—figure supplement 2), suggesting that EFA-6 and UNC-75 function in parallel.
evidence: This is inferred from genetic interaction data (Figure 1—figure supplement 2, 3C).

claim: dlk-1 and efa-6 transcript levels were normal in unc-75 mutants.
source: Moreover, dlk-1 and efa-6 transcript levels were normal in unc-75 mutants (Figure 1—figure supplement 3D).
evidence: RT-qPCR data is shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3D.

claim: The UNC-75 axon extension pathway acts partly independently of the DLK-1 and EFA-6 axon regeneration regulators.
source: Thus, these analyses suggest the UNC-75 axon extension pathway acts partly independently of the DLK-1 and EFA-6 axon regeneration regulators.
evidence: This is inferred from genetic interaction data and transcript level measurements (Figure 1—figure supplement 3).

claim: 533 functionally annotated protein-coding genes were identified as UNC-75 targets through CLIP-seq.
source: We identified 533 functionally annotated protein-coding genes as UNC-75 targets (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is based on CLIP-seq analysis described in the methods and shown in Figure 2A.

claim: 79% of the UNC-75 CLIP peaks in protein-coding genes were in intronic regions.
source: 79% of the peaks in protein-coding genes were in intronic regions, and 21% in exons or UTRs, consistent with previous results implicating UNC-75 in alternative splicing (Kuroyanagi et al., 2013a; 2013b; Norris et al., 2014).
evidence: This is based on analysis of CLIP-seq data and is consistent with cited previous work.

claim: The most enriched UNC-75 binding motif was UGUGUGUG.
source: The most enriched motif was UGUGUGUG, as exemplified by the binding site on unc-75 mRNA (Figure 2C), consistent with the UNC-75 binding site (G/U)UGUUGUG previously inferred from RNA-seq (Kuroyanagi et al., 2013b) and the U(G/A)UUGUG consensus motif defined by RNAcompete (Norris et al., 2014).
evidence: This is based on MEME analysis of CLIP-seq data (Figure 2B) and is consistent with cited previous work.

claim: The second most enriched UNC-75 binding motif is G/CAAAAAA.
source: The second most enriched motif G/CAAAAAA is not previously known, and is exemplified by nrx-1, a known UNC-75 target (Kuroyanagi et al., 2013b; Norris et al., 2014) (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is based on MEME analysis of CLIP-seq data (Figure 2B, C).

claim: The list of putative UNC-75 targets identified in CLIP-seq analysis showed significant overlap with those identified in comparisons of whole-organism transcriptomes of wild type and unc-75 mutants.
source: The list of putative UNC-75 targets identified in our CLIP-seq analysis showed significant overlap with those identified in comparisons of whole-organism transcriptomes of wild type and unc-75 mutants (Kuroyanagi et al., 2013b; Norris et al., 2014) (Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This comparison is shown in Supplementary file 2.

claim: UNC-75 binding sites in introns often overlapped with regions that express snoRNAs.
source: When manually checking the genomic loci of UNC-75 targets, we observed that UNC-75 binding sites in introns often overlapped with regions that express snoRNAs.
evidence: An example is shown in Figure 2C where peak s5644 in unc-41 overlaps with snoRNA C27H6.5.

claim: The three most enriched functional annotation clusters for UNC-75 targets are alternative splicing, nucleotide-binding, and transmembrane.
source: The three most enriched functional annotation clusters are alternative splicing (49 genes, P = 3.9E-20, Fisher's exact test), nucleotide-binding (60 genes, P = 4.5E-17) and transmembrane (66 genes, P = 2.2E-12), consistent with previously reported functions of UNC-75 in alternative splicing, and validating the quality of our CLIP-seq.
evidence: This is based on Gene Ontology analysis using DAVID on the 533 UNC-75 targets.

claim: The most significantly enriched signaling network for UNC-75 targets is MAPK pathway.
source: The most significantly enriched signaling network is MAPK pathway (9 genes, P = 4.7E-3).
evidence: This is based on Gene Ontology analysis using DAVID on the 533 UNC-75 targets.

claim: Among the 533 protein-coding target genes of UNC-75, 17 genes were previously identified as required for axon regeneration.
source: Among the 533 protein-coding target genes of UNC-75, we found 17 genes previously identified as required for axon regeneration (Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This is based on comparison with a previous genetic screen (Chen et al., 2011).

claim: The most significantly enriched cluster among 17 UNC-75 targets required for regeneration is cholinergic synaptic transmission.
source: GO analysis on these 17 genes resulted in the most significantly enriched cluster as cholinergic synaptic transmission (P = 1.6E-6, 4 genes including unc-32, unc-41, unc-64, unc-75 and unc-104).
evidence: This is based on Gene Ontology analysis on the 17 genes.

claim: Mutants of synaptic transmission genes have normal PLM axon outgrowth in development and display significantly reduced PLM regrowth.
source: Mutants of these genes have normal PLM axon outgrowth in development and display significantly reduced PLM regrowth (Chen et al., 2011), yet their injured PLM axons were able to form regenerative growth cone-like structures more often than wild type axons (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work and data in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: Synaptic transmission genes are specifically required for efficient regenerative axon extension.
source: Thus, these synaptic transmission genes, like unc-75, appear to be specifically required for efficient regenerative axon extension.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that these mutants form growth cones but fail to extend efficiently (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).

claim: A prominent UNC-75 CLIP-seq peak mapped to the last intron (intron 7) of unc-64.
source: To understand how UNC-75 regulates its targets, we chose unc-64/Syntaxin for further study, as a prominent UNC-75 CLIP-seq peak mapped to the last intron (intron 7) of unc-64 (Figure 3A).
evidence: CLIP-seq data showing the peak is displayed in Figure 3A.

claim: Alternative splicing of unc-64 exons 8a and 8b generates transcripts encoding UNC-64A and UNC-64B isoforms, which differ in their C-terminal hydrophobic membrane anchors.
source: Alternative splicing of unc-64 exons 8a and 8b, which flank intron 7b, generates transcripts encoding UNC-64A and UNC-64B isoforms, which differ in their C-terminal hydrophobic membrane anchors (Ogawa et al., 1998; Saifee et al., 1998).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: UNC-64A is expressed predominantly in neurons and in some non-neuronal tissues.
source: UNC-64A is expressed predominantly in neurons and in some non-neuronal tissues, whereas UNC-64B is only expressed in non-neuronal tissues (Saifee et al., 1998) (Figure 3B,C).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work and reporter expression data in Figure 3B, C.

claim: UNC-64B is only expressed in non-neuronal tissues.
source: UNC-64A is expressed predominantly in neurons and in some non-neuronal tissues, whereas UNC-64B is only expressed in non-neuronal tissues (Saifee et al., 1998) (Figure 3B,C).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work and reporter expression data in Figure 3B, C.

claim: unc-64A mRNAs were significantly reduced in unc-75 mutants.
source: RT-qPCR analyses showed that unc-64A mRNAs were significantly reduced in unc-75 mutants, whereas unc-64B mRNAs were increased (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: RT-qPCR data is shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.

claim: unc-64B mRNAs were increased in unc-75 mutants.
source: RT-qPCR analyses showed that unc-64A mRNAs were significantly reduced in unc-75 mutants, whereas unc-64B mRNAs were increased (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: RT-qPCR data is shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Total unc-64 mRNA levels were reduced in unc-75 mutants compared to wild type.
source: Total unc-64 mRNA levels were reduced in unc-75 mutants compared to wild type, and expression of UNC-64 proteins in neurons was strongly reduced as determined by immunostaining using antibodies that recognize both isoforms (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: RT-qPCR and immunostaining data are shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A, B.

claim: Expression of UNC-64 proteins in neurons was strongly reduced in unc-75 mutants.
source: Total unc-64 mRNA levels were reduced in unc-75 mutants compared to wild type, and expression of UNC-64 proteins in neurons was strongly reduced as determined by immunostaining using antibodies that recognize both isoforms (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Immunostaining data is shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B.

claim: UNC-75 is required for neuronal expression of UNC-64/Syntaxin isoforms.
source: Thus, UNC-75 is required for neuronal expression of UNC-64/Syntaxin isoforms.
evidence: This is inferred from RT-qPCR and immunostaining data (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).

claim: In unc-75(0) mutants UNC-64A::GFP is expressed at lower levels in most neurons.
source: In wild-type animals, UNC-64A::GFP is strongly expressed in most neurons. In unc-75(0) mutants UNC-64A::GFP is expressed at lower levels in most neurons.
evidence: Reporter expression data is shown in Figure 3B with quantification.

claim: UNC-64B::GFP is not expressed in the nervous system in wild-type background but is ectopically expressed in head neurons in unc-75(0).
source: UNC-64B::GFP is not expressed in the nervous system in wild-type background but is ectopically expressed in head neurons in unc-75(0).
evidence: Reporter expression data is shown in Figure 3C with quantification.

claim: Deletion of the 38 bp UNC-75 binding site in intron 7 results in neuronal expression of UNC-64B::GFP in wild-type background.
source: Deletion of the 38 bp UNC-75 binding site in intron 7 results in neuronal expression of UNC-64B::GFP in wild-type background.
evidence: Reporter expression data is shown in Figure 3D with quantification.

claim: In unc-75 mutants, neuronal RFP expression (UNC-64A-like) was greatly reduced and GFP expression (UNC-64B-like) was increased in neurons using a dual splicing reporter.
source: In a wild type background, these transgenic animals expressed RFP strongly in the nervous system (UNC-64A-like expression), whereas GFP (reflecting the UNC-64B isoform) was undetectable. In unc-75 mutants, neuronal RFP expression was greatly reduced and GFP expression was increased in neurons (Figure 3E).
evidence: Dual reporter expression data is shown in Figure 3E with quantification.

claim: By RNA-seq, significantly more reads mapping to intron 7a of unc-64 were detected in unc-75 mutants, and fewer reads mapping to intron 7b compared to wild type.
source: In addition, by RNA-seq, we detected significantly more reads mapping to intron 7a of unc-64 in unc-75 mutants, and fewer reads mapping to intron 7b compared to wild type (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: RNA-seq data is shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: UNC-75 binding in intron 7 promotes alternative splicing of exon 8a and represses inclusion of exon 8b through intron retention, resulting in neuronal expression of UNC-64A and repression of UNC-64B.
source: These analyses suggest UNC-75 binding in intron 7 promotes alternative splicing of exon 8a and represses inclusion of exon 8b through intron retention, resulting in neuronal expression of UNC-64A and repression of UNC-64B.
evidence: This is inferred from multiple lines of evidence including CLIP-seq, reporter assays, and RNA-seq (Figure 3).

claim: A premature stop codon mutation (js116) in the UNC-64A transmembrane domain causes complete loss of function.
source: A premature stop codon mutation (js116) in the UNC-64A transmembrane domain causes complete loss of function, indicating the importance of this domain (Saifee et al., 1998).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Expression of UNC-64 lacking a transmembrane domain (UNC-64ΔTM) was unable to rescue the movement defect of unc-64(md130).
source: Consistent with this, expression of UNC-64 lacking a transmembrane domain (UNC-64ΔTM) was unable to rescue the movement defect of unc-64(md130) (Figure 3—figure supplement 3), a partial loss of function (plf) allele affecting both isoforms (van Swinderen et al., 1999).
evidence: Rescue data is shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3.

claim: Pan-neuronal expression of UNC-64A, but not of UNC-64B, was able to rescue the locomotion defects of unc-64(plf).
source: We further expressed specific isoforms using cDNAs, and found that pan-neuronal expression of UNC-64A, but not of UNC-64B, was able to rescue the locomotion defects of unc-64(plf) (Figure 3—figure supplement 3).
evidence: Rescue data is shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3.

claim: UNC-64A appears to be the major functional Syntaxin isoform in neurons.
source: Thus UNC-64A appears to be the major functional Syntaxin isoform in neurons; even when ectopically expressed in neurons, as in unc-75 mutants, UNC-64B is unable to substitute for UNC-64A.
evidence: This is inferred from rescue experiments showing UNC-64A but not UNC-64B can rescue locomotion defects (Figure 3—figure supplement 3).

claim: Even when ectopically expressed in neurons, UNC-64B is unable to substitute for UNC-64A.
source: Thus UNC-64A appears to be the major functional Syntaxin isoform in neurons; even when ectopically expressed in neurons, as in unc-75 mutants, UNC-64B is unable to substitute for UNC-64A.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that unc-75 mutants have ectopic UNC-64B expression but still show defects (Figure 3C).

claim: Partial loss of function in unc-64 (md130 or e246) results in a partial block in PLM axon regeneration.
source: Partial loss of function in unc-64 (md130 or e246) results in a partial block in PLM axon regeneration (Figure 4A).
evidence: Quantitative data is shown in Figure 4A.

claim: unc-64(js115) null mutants arrest in the first larval stage.
source: As unc-64(js115) null mutants arrest in the first larval stage (Saifee et al., 1998), we used two approaches to examine the null phenotype of unc-64 in regeneration.
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: In unc-64(js115) null mutants rescued for lethality, PLM developed normally and axon regeneration was inhibited to a similar extent as in unc-64(plf).
source: We first tested unc-64(js115) null mutants in which lethality, but not movement, was rescued by expression of UNC-64 under the combined control of acr-2, unc-17, and glr-1 promoters (Hammarlund et al., 2007). In such animals PLM developed normally and axon regeneration was inhibited to a similar extent as in unc-64(plf) (Figure 4A).
evidence: Quantitative data is shown in Figure 4A.

claim: The unc-64(0) PLM axons developed normally.
source: The unc-64(0) PLM axons developed normally (Figure 4—figure supplement 1) and displayed reduced regrowth after axotomy, comparable to unc-64(plf) (Figure 4A).
evidence: Images of PLM development are shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: UNC-64 is specifically required for axon regeneration but not development.
source: We conclude that UNC-64 is specifically required for axon regeneration but not development, and that the null phenotype of unc-64 is a partial block in regeneration.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that unc-64 null mutants have normal PLM development but defective regeneration (Figure 4A, Figure 4—figure supplement 1).

claim: The null phenotype of unc-64 is a partial block in regeneration.
source: We conclude that UNC-64 is specifically required for axon regeneration but not development, and that the null phenotype of unc-64 is a partial block in regeneration.
evidence: This is based on quantitative data showing partial reduction in regeneration in unc-64 null mutants (Figure 4A).

claim: Regenerative growth cones in unc-64(md130) mutants had dynamic filopodia but did not effectively elongate.
source: Regenerative growth cones in unc-64(md130) mutants had dynamic filopodia but did not effectively elongate, resembling those of unc-75(0) (Video 3).
evidence: This is shown through time-lapse imaging in Video 3.

claim: Regrowth defects in unc-64(md130) were rescued by pan-neuronal expression of either UNC-64A or UNC-64B.
source: Moreover, regrowth defects in unc-64(md130) were rescued by pan-neuronal expression of either UNC-64A or UNC-64B (Figure 4A), suggesting either isoform is sufficient for function in regeneration when overexpressed.
evidence: Quantitative rescue data is shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Either UNC-64 isoform is sufficient for function in regeneration when overexpressed.
source: Moreover, regrowth defects in unc-64(md130) were rescued by pan-neuronal expression of either UNC-64A or UNC-64B (Figure 4A), suggesting either isoform is sufficient for function in regeneration when overexpressed.
evidence: This is inferred from rescue experiments (Figure 4A).

claim: Transgenes containing unc-64 genomic DNA significantly suppressed the PLM regeneration defects of unc-75 mutants.
source: Strikingly, transgenes containing unc-64 genomic DNA, which produce both UNC-64A and UNC-64B, significantly suppressed the PLM regeneration defects of unc-75 mutants (Figure 5A,B).
evidence: Quantitative rescue data is shown in Figure 5A, B.

claim: Pan-neuronal overexpression of UNC-64A (using cDNA), but not of UNC-64B, rescued unc-75 regeneration defects.
source: Furthermore, pan-neuronal overexpression of UNC-64A (using cDNA), but not of UNC-64B, rescued unc-75 regeneration defects to a similar degree as unc-64 genomic DNA, whereas UNC-64ΔTM did not rescue (Figure 5A,B).
evidence: Quantitative rescue data is shown in Figure 5A, B.

claim: Transgenes expressing unc-64 genomic DNA or UNC-64A strongly suppressed unc-75 locomotor phenotypes.
source: Moreover, transgenes expressing unc-64 genomic DNA or UNC-64A strongly suppressed unc-75 locomotor phenotypes, while overexpression of UNC-64B or UNC-64ΔTM did not rescue (Figure 5C,D).
evidence: Quantitative locomotion data is shown in Figure 5C, D.

claim: Decreased neuronal expression of the UNC-64A isoform is a major contributor to unc-75 mutant phenotypes in regeneration and behavior.
source: We infer that decreased neuronal expression of the UNC-64A isoform is a major contributor to unc-75 mutant phenotypes in regeneration and behavior.
evidence: This is inferred from rescue experiments showing UNC-64A overexpression suppresses unc-75 defects (Figure 5).

claim: Mouse CELF2 or CELF4, when expressed in C. elegans touch neurons, could significantly rescue the unc-75 PLM regrowth defect.
source: Here, we found that either mouse CELF2 or CELF4, when expressed in C. elegans touch neurons, could significantly rescue the unc-75 PLM regrowth defect, with CELF2 being slightly more effective than CELF4 (Figure 6A).
evidence: Quantitative rescue data is shown in Figure 6A.

claim: CELF2 is generally localized in the nucleus in neurons.
source: This may be because CELF2, like UNC-75, is generally localized in the nucleus in neurons (Otsuka et al., 2009) whereas CELF4 is predominantly cytoplasmic (Wagnon et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: CELF4 is predominantly cytoplasmic.
source: This may be because CELF2, like UNC-75, is generally localized in the nucleus in neurons (Otsuka et al., 2009) whereas CELF4 is predominantly cytoplasmic (Wagnon et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: CELF proteins may play a conserved role in axon regeneration.
source: Nonetheless, this result suggests that the CELF proteins may also play a conserved role in axon regeneration.
evidence: This is inferred from the ability of mammalian CELF proteins to rescue C. elegans unc-75 defects (Figure 6A).

claim: Celf2 transcript levels in DRG neurons decrease during postnatal development.
source: Celf4 transcripts increased during postnatal development (Figure 6B), consistent with reported expression (Supplementary file 3). In contrast, Celf2 mRNA levels declined from perinatal stages to adult (Figure 6B).
evidence: RT-qPCR data is shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Celf4 transcripts increased during postnatal development.
source: Celf4 transcripts increased during postnatal development (Figure 6B), consistent with reported expression (Supplementary file 3).
evidence: RT-qPCR data is shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Celf2 transcript levels significantly increased in DRGs after sciatic nerve crush in 2-month old animals.
source: Notably, Celf2 transcript levels significantly increased in DRGs after sciatic nerve crush in 2-month old animals (Figure 6C).
evidence: RT-qPCR data is shown in Figure 6C.

claim: The developmental decline in Celf2 expression and its upregulation after injury suggest Celf2 expression correlates with axon regeneration capacity.
source: As the peripheral processes of DRG neurons are capable of regeneration, and such capacity declines with age (Mar et al., 2014), the developmental decline in Celf2 expression and its upregulation after injury suggest Celf2 expression correlates with axon regeneration capacity.
evidence: This is inferred from expression patterns (Figure 6B, C) and cited knowledge about age-related decline in regeneration capacity.

claim: Constitutive Celf2-/- mice died neonatally, with 5% escapers surviving up to 3 weeks.
source: These constitutive Celf2-/- mice died neonatally, with 5% escapers surviving up to 3 weeks.
evidence: This is an observation from generating and characterizing the Celf2 knockout mice.

claim: No obvious morphological defects were detected in newborn Celf2-/- animals by histological analysis.
source: No obvious morphological defects were detected in newborn Celf2-/- animals by histological analysis (not shown).
evidence: This is stated as an observation from characterizing the Celf2 knockout mice.

claim: Explants of DRG neurons derived from E13.5 Celf2-/- embryos displayed significantly reduced axon extension.
source: Explants of DRG neurons derived from E13.5 Celf2-/- embryos displayed significantly reduced axon extension (Figure 6—figure supplement 1C,D).
evidence: Quantitative data from DRG explant cultures is shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1C, D.

claim: Celf2 does not seem to play a major role in developmental axon outgrowth.
source: Thus although Celf2 does not seem to play a major role in developmental axon outgrowth, it is required for efficient regrowth of axons from explants.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that Celf2 mutants show defects in explant regrowth but no obvious developmental defects.

claim: Celf2 is required for efficient regrowth of axons from explants.
source: Thus although Celf2 does not seem to play a major role in developmental axon outgrowth, it is required for efficient regrowth of axons from explants.
evidence: This is based on data from DRG explant cultures (Figure 6—figure supplement 1C, D).

claim: Nestin-Cre induced Celf2 knockout animals were smaller than littermates and usually survived 1–2 months.
source: Nestin-Cre induced Celf2 knockout animals were smaller than littermates (Figure 6—figure supplement 1E) and usually survived 1–2 months.
evidence: This is an observation from characterizing the conditional Celf2 knockout mice (Figure 6—figure supplement 1E).

claim: Celf2 knockout neurons showed defects in adult DRG regeneration after re-suspension and re-plating of DRG cells.
source: Using an in vitro regeneration assay (Saijilafu and Zhou, 2012), we found Celf2 knockout neurons showed defects in adult DRG regeneration after re-suspension and re-plating of DRG cells (Figure 6—figure supplement 1F,G).
evidence: Quantitative data from in vitro regeneration assays is shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1F, G.

claim: SCG10 positive DRG axons distal to the crush site were significantly reduced in the Celf2 mutant compared to littermate controls.
source: SCG10 positive DRG axons distal to the crush site were significantly reduced in the Celf2 mutant compared to littermate controls (Figure 6C,D), indicating that CELF2 is required for DRG axon regeneration.
evidence: Quantitative data from in vivo sciatic nerve regeneration is shown in Figure 6D, E.

claim: CELF2 is required for DRG axon regeneration.
source: SCG10 positive DRG axons distal to the crush site were significantly reduced in the Celf2 mutant compared to littermate controls (Figure 6C,D), indicating that CELF2 is required for DRG axon regeneration.
evidence: This is inferred from in vivo regeneration data (Figure 6D, E).

claim: CELF proteins play a conserved role in axon regeneration from C. elegans to mouse.
source: Together, these data support a conclusion that CELF proteins play a conserved role in axon regeneration from C. elegans to mouse.
evidence: This is inferred from data showing both UNC-75 and CELF2 are required for axon regeneration in their respective organisms (Figures 1, 6).

claim: 2919 protein coding genes were identified as CELF2 targets through CLIP-seq.
source: We identified 2919 protein coding genes as CELF2 targets (Supplementary file 4) and 'UGUGUGUG' as the most significant binding motif, which is conserved to UNC-75, suggesting the function of CELF genes in target regulation is highly conserved.
evidence: This is based on CELF2 CLIP-seq analysis in N2A cells.

claim: 'UGUGUGUG' is the most significant CELF2 binding motif.
source: We identified 2919 protein coding genes as CELF2 targets (Supplementary file 4) and 'UGUGUGUG' as the most significant binding motif, which is conserved to UNC-75, suggesting the function of CELF genes in target regulation is highly conserved.
evidence: This is based on motif analysis of CELF2 CLIP-seq data.

claim: The CELF2 binding motif is conserved to UNC-75.
source: We identified 2919 protein coding genes as CELF2 targets (Supplementary file 4) and 'UGUGUGUG' as the most significant binding motif, which is conserved to UNC-75, suggesting the function of CELF genes in target regulation is highly conserved.
evidence: This is based on comparison of motifs from UNC-75 and CELF2 CLIP-seq (Figure 2B and text).

claim: The function of CELF genes in target regulation is highly conserved.
source: We identified 2919 protein coding genes as CELF2 targets (Supplementary file 4) and 'UGUGUGUG' as the most significant binding motif, which is conserved to UNC-75, suggesting the function of CELF genes in target regulation is highly conserved.
evidence: This is inferred from the conservation of binding motifs and functional rescue experiments.

claim: CELF2 binding sites were identified in multiple mouse Syntaxin genes from CLIP-seq.
source: From CELF2 CLIP-seq we identified CELF2 binding sites in multiple mouse Syntaxin genes (Figure 7A and Supplementary file 4).
evidence: CLIP-seq data is shown in Figure 7A and Supplementary file 4.

claim: mRNA levels of splicing variants of Syntaxin2 and Syntaxin16 were significantly altered in Celf2-/- mouse brain.
source: We examined expression of candidate Syntaxin genes in Celf2 knockout mouse brain by RT-qPCR, and observed that mRNA levels of splicing variants of Syntaxin2 and Syntaxin16 were significantly altered in Celf2-/- mouse brain (Figure 7B).
evidence: RT-qPCR data is shown in Figure 7B.

claim: Syntaxin2 is ubiquitously expressed.
source: Syntaxin2 is ubiquitously expressed (Bennett et al., 1993), but its role in the nervous system is not known.
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Syntaxin2 is alternatively spliced, generating two isoforms differing in the C-terminal membrane anchor.
source: Reminiscent of unc-64, Syntaxin2 is alternatively spliced, generating two isoforms differing in the C-terminal membrane anchor.
evidence: This is inferred from CLIP-seq data showing CELF2 binding near alternatively spliced exons (Figure 7A).

claim: A CELF2 binding site was found in the intron 5' to the alternatively spliced exons of Syntaxin2.
source: From CLIP-seq we found a CELF2 binding site in the intron 5' to the alternatively spliced exons (Figure 7A).
evidence: CLIP-seq data is shown in Figure 7A.

claim: Syntaxin16 expression is enriched in neurons in the brain and has been implicated in neurite growth.
source: Syntaxin16 expression is enriched in neurons in the brain and has been implicated in neurite growth (Chua and Tang, 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Two splicing variants of Syntaxin16 differ in exons encoding the N terminus.
source: Two splicing variants of Syntaxin16 differ in exons encoding the N terminus, which is known to interact with Vps45 (Dulubova et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: CELF2 binding was detected on the introns in the immediate vicinity to the alternatively spliced exons of Syntaxin16, as well as on the 3' UTR.
source: We detected CELF2 binding on the introns in the immediate vicinity to the alternatively spliced exons, as well as on the 3' UTR (Figure 7A).
evidence: CLIP-seq data is shown in Figure 7A.

claim: CELF-mediated regulation of alternative splicing of Syntaxin genes is likely a conserved mechanism in axon regeneration.
source: Taken together, these data support a hypothesis that CELF-mediated regulation of alternative splicing of Syntaxin genes is likely a conserved mechanism in axon regeneration.
evidence: This is inferred from data showing CELF regulation of Syntaxins in both C. elegans and mouse (Figures 3, 7).

claim: Expression of neuronal Syntaxins is regulated by CELF-mediated alternative splicing and is critical for regeneration.
source: Expression of neuronal Syntaxins is regulated by CELF-mediated alternative splicing and is critical for regeneration.
evidence: This is based on data showing CELF regulation of Syntaxin splicing and the requirement of Syntaxins for regeneration (Figures 3-5, 7).

claim: The CELF/Syntaxin pathway is not required for regenerative growth cones to form but allows them to efficiently extend axons.
source: The CELF/Syntaxin pathway is not required for regenerative growth cones to form but allows them to efficiently extend axons.
evidence: This is based on observations that unc-75 and unc-64 mutants form growth cones but fail to extend (Figures 1, 4, Videos 1-3).

claim: Post-transcriptional regulation by CELF balances the production of mRNA and protein isoforms during axonal regeneration.
source: We propose that post-transcriptional regulation by CELF balances the production of mRNA and protein isoforms during axonal regeneration.
evidence: This is a proposed model based on the data showing CELF regulation of alternative splicing affects regeneration.
